The bill would change the Interactive Gambling Act 2001 to target illegal offshore wagering.
It would give the Australian Communications and Media Authority new powers to enforce a licensing requirement and impose civil penalties.
The bill would ban 'click-to-call' in-play betting services, where a customer places a bet during a sport without speaking to a human operator.
Clarifies the types of gambling services the Act applies to, distinguishing prohibited from regulated services.
Creates a civil penalty and enforcement regime for the ACMA.
Allows the ACMA to share information with the Department of Immigration and Border Protection and foreign regulators.
Simplifies complaints handling and investigation processes.
Establishes a register of eligible regulated interactive gambling services.
Offshore wagering providers, Australian wagering, hospitality and sporting industries, problem gamblers, consumers, and the Australian Communications and Media Authority.

This is something that I know is contentious, but if you want this to work it can work. We know from just one company, Netsweeper of Canada, that I met with and that have given submissions to inquiries in relation to this that you can have internet content filtering categorisation, web threat management solutions and services that allow organisations to manage internet access and activity. If they are fair dinkum about clamping down on multinationals in Australia—in this case not employing a lot of Australians—taking money out of the country by not paying taxes here, then I expect the government and the opposition to support my amendments. The Interactive Gambling Amendment Bill was introduced as the first stage of implementing 18 of the 19 recommendations from the 2015 illegal offshore wagering review, aiming to strengthen enforcement against illegal online gambling by clarifying licensing requirements, banning 'click to call' in-play betting, and empowering the ACMA with civil penalties, infringement notices, and a public register of licensed Australian wagering services.

Labor supported the Interactive Gambling Amendment Bill 2016 as a first step to curb illegal offshore gambling, citing $1.4 billion in annual online losses and 800,000 active wagering accounts by 2014. The party moved a second reading amendment calling for a transition plan to phase out gambling advertising during live sports broadcasts, and criticised the government for not banning credit betting.

The Interactive Gambling Amendment Bill 2016 strengthens enforcement against illegal offshore gambling operators, including their Australian-based agents and affiliates, and introduces a civil penalty regime enforced by the Australian Communications and Media Authority. The bill responds to a review led by Barry O'Farrell, noting that Australians spent $2.4 billion on online gambling in 2014 and up to $400 million annually on illegal wagering, with the aim of reducing harm and protecting consumers, racing industries, and tax revenue.

Labor announced a second reading amendment to the Interactive Gambling Amendment Bill 2016, calling for a transition plan to phase out betting odds promotion and gambling commercials during live sports broadcasts, citing a 251% increase in gambling ads since 2013 and that three in four children aged 8–16 could recall a sports betting brand.

The Interactive Gambling Amendment Bill 2016 aims to curb illegal international online gambling, which siphons $400 million annually from Australia and threatens the regulated racing industry that supports 250,000 jobs. The government adopted 18 of Barry O'Farrell's 19 recommendations, citing that online problem gambling rates are three times higher than other forms and that the sector is growing at 15 per cent per year.

The speaker supported the Interactive Gambling Amendment Bill 2016 and the Franklin amendment, citing rapid growth in online wagering accounts (200,000 to 800,000, 2004–2014) and Australians' highest per-adult gambling losses globally, while calling for a transition plan to phase out gambling ads during live sports to protect children and vulnerable people.

The Interactive Gambling Amendment Bill 2016 implements key recommendations from a review led by Barry O'Farrell, including cracking down on illegal offshore gambling, prohibiting click-to-call in-play betting, and establishing a national consumer protection framework. The bill empowers ACMA with civil penalties and introduces measures such as a movement alert list for offending company directors, targeting an estimated $64–400 million annually lost to illegal offshore sites.

The Labor MP argued for a transition plan to phase out gambling advertising during live sports broadcasts to prevent children from associating gambling with sport, and supported the Interactive Gambling Amendment Bill to address illegal offshore online gambling, noting that $140 million is spent annually on gambling ads and problem gambling affects around 90,000 Australians.

The Interactive Gambling Amendment Bill 2016 will prohibit 'click to call' in-play betting, strengthen enforcement against illegal offshore gambling, and empower ACMA, with the speaker supporting an amendment to phase out gambling advertising during live sports broadcasts, citing that 75% of children view gambling as normal and 80% of respondents back restrictions.

The speaker supported the Interactive Gambling Amendment Bill 2016 and an amendment to phase out betting odds promotions during live sports broadcasts, citing concerns over children being exposed to gambling ads, such as an eight-year-old quoting odds. The bill introduces civil penalties enforced by ACMA, prohibits click-to-call in-play betting, and establishes a register of legitimate gambling services.

Labor supported the Interactive Gambling Amendment Bill 2016, including a ban on credit betting and a $30 million turnover threshold for trackside bookmaker exemptions, and urged the government to prevent other operators from exploiting loopholes.

The minister inadvertently failed to table the supplementary explanatory memorandum during debate on the Interactive Gambling Amendment Bill 2016; the speaker then presented the document for the information of members, covering government amendments already agreed to by the House.
